title: Which change justifies an emergency review
question: Your team relaxes normal review depth only for genuine emergencies. Four authors ask for a same-day rubber-stamp approval. Following Google's review guidance, which request actually qualifies?
options: A feature the author has spent two months on and wants merged before a vacation
A change that must ship by Friday evening so that Monday's sprint demo looks complete
A small patch that closes an actively exploited authentication bypass in production
A refactor the manager wants merged today because of a soft target set at planning
explanation: Google's guidance limits emergencies to small changes such as closing a major security hole, fixing a bug that badly hurts production users, letting a major launch continue, or handling a pressing legal issue. Long-running work, end-of-week convenience and soft managerial deadlines are explicitly not emergencies, so those changes get the normal review standard.

title: After an emergency fix lands
question: During an outage you approved a hotfix after checking only that it stopped the failing payments and looked correct. The incident is now resolved. What does Google's review guidance expect next?
options: Look over the emergency change again and give it a more thorough review
Nothing further, because the fix has already gone through code review
Revert the hotfix and reapply it later as a regular, fully reviewed PR
Leave it to QA sign-off, since a reviewer has already seen the diff once
explanation: In an emergency the reviewer may focus mainly on speed and on whether the change actually resolves the emergency, but the guidance says to look over emergency changes again once things are resolved and give them a more thorough review. Reverting a working fix adds risk, and skipping the follow-up leaves code in place that never met the normal standard.

title: Well-built code for an unwanted feature
question: A PR adds a built-in cron scheduler to your HTTP routing library. The code is clean, tested and well designed, but the maintainers have decided that scheduling does not belong in this library. What is the appropriate review outcome?
options: Approve it, since the standard favors approval whenever code health improves
Approve it with nits, and open an issue to discuss the library's scope later
Request more tests first, then approve once coverage reaches the team target
Decline it and explain the scope decision, though the code itself is good
explanation: The 'approve when it improves code health' rule has explicit limits: if a change adds a feature the reviewer does not want in the system, they can deny approval even when the code is well designed. Design includes whether the change belongs in this codebase at all, so asking for more tests or approving now and debating later both miss the real problem.

title: Two equally valid designs
question: You would have used a strategy interface; the author used a small switch over an enum. The author shows a benchmark and a short argument that both are equally maintainable for the three cases that exist. How should the disagreement be settled?
options: The reviewer's choice wins, because reviewers own the design of the codebase
Accept the author's approach, since they showed both options are valid
Ask a third engineer to vote, and go with whichever option gets two votes
Require the strategy interface anyway, because it is the more extensible one
explanation: Google's standard says design is weighed on engineering principles, not opinion, and when the author demonstrates with data or solid principles that several approaches are equally valid, the reviewer should accept the author's preference. Insisting on extensibility for cases that do not exist yet is personal preference, and voting replaces reasoning with a headcount.

title: Approving when you reviewed only part
question: A 12-file PR has three reviewers. You were asked to review only the authentication changes in two files, and they look good. What should your approval convey?
options: Approve, noting in a comment which parts of the change you actually reviewed
Approve silently, since the merge rules count approvals and not their scope
Hold approval until you have personally gone through all twelve of the files
Leave a plain comment instead of approving, so you are not responsible for it
explanation: When you are asked to review only certain files or aspects of a change, the guidance says to note in a comment which parts you reviewed and to prefer LGTM with comments. A silent approval suggests you vouched for the whole change, while withholding or refusing approval slows the author down without adding any review value.

title: Every release ends in a review rush
question: Releases ship every six weeks. In the last two days of each cycle, large feature PRs arrive that 'must get in', get a superficial review, and the codebase is accumulating debt. What is the best fix according to Google's review guidance?
options: Treat the final two days as an emergency window with a lighter review bar
Add more reviewers in the final week so the big PRs get skimmed in parallel
Change the process so large features land early, with time for review
Extend the cycle to eight weeks so that more features fit before the cutoff
explanation: The guidance warns that routinely pushing 'must get in' changes through superficial review near a release cut is a common way to build overwhelming technical debt, and recommends changing the process so large feature work happens early in the cycle with enough time for good review. Release targets are usually soft deadlines, not emergencies, and longer cycles or more skimmers just move the same rush around.

title: When 200 lines is too big
question: Two PRs each change about 200 lines. PR A edits one file; PR B touches 50 files with a few lines each. How does Google's small-CL guidance view them?
options: Both are fine, because size is judged only by the number of changed lines
PR A is likely fine, while PR B is usually too large because of its spread
Both are too large, since anything over 100 changed lines should be split
PR B is better, since tiny edits per file are easier for reviewers to follow
explanation: The guidance treats 100 lines as usually reasonable and 1000 as usually too large, but says the number of files also affects size: a 200-line change in one file might be fine, while the same lines spread across 50 files usually is too large. Line count alone is not a hard rule, and scattered edits force the reviewer to rebuild context dozens of times.

title: A new API with no callers yet
question: To keep PRs small, an author sends PR 1 adding a public `RateLimiter.TryAcquire(key, cost)` API with unit tests, and plans to add the first caller in PR 2 next week. What should the reviewer ask for?
options: Nothing; an unused API is the ideal small change and the easiest to review
Merge the API now, but mark it internal until PR 2 actually starts using it
Combine both PRs and also add the feature flag, the docs and the dashboard
Include a real usage in the same PR so the API's shape can be judged
explanation: Google's guidance warns that a change can be so small that its implications are hard to understand: when you add a new API, include a usage of it in the same change so reviewers can judge how it will be used, which also avoids checking in unused APIs. Bundling everything else back in overshoots, and changing visibility does not help the reviewer evaluate the design.

title: Bug fix hidden inside a move and rename
question: A PR moves `InvoiceCalc.cs` to a new folder, renames the class to `InvoiceCalculator`, and fixes a rounding bug inside it. The diff shows the whole old file deleted and a new file added. What is the best review request?
options: Split it: the move and rename in one PR, then the rounding fix in another
Approve, since a rename is mechanical and the tool shows the full new file
Ask the author to describe the rounding fix in detail in the description
Ask for the rounding fix to wait until the next planned refactoring sprint
explanation: Refactorings such as moving and renaming a class should go in a separate change from bug fixes in that class; mixed together, the fix is buried in a delete-and-add diff that nobody can review line by line. A description helps but does not make the logic change visible, and delaying a real bug fix for process reasons is not the goal.

title: A 3,000-line PR from a codemod
question: An engineer runs the team's trusted automated refactoring tool to rename a widely used method, producing a 3,000-line PR with no hand edits. How should reviewers treat its size?
options: Reject it outright, since anything above 1,000 lines is too big to review
Ask for it to be split into 30 PRs of 100 lines each to meet the guideline
Accept the size; the job is mainly to confirm that the change is wanted
Review every line with the same depth as hand-written business logic
explanation: The small-CL guidance names large changes generated by an automatic refactoring tool you trust completely as an acceptable exception: the reviewer's job is mostly to verify that they really want the change. Splitting a mechanical rename into arbitrary chunks adds merge and build risk without improving the review, although caveats such as merging and testing still apply.

title: Stacked PRs that break main in between
question: An author splits a migration into a stack: PR 1 deletes the old `GetUserAsync(int)` overload, PR 2 updates its 14 callers to the new overload. PR 1 is approved first and the author wants to merge it right away. What is the problem?
options: None; stacked PRs are always merged in order, so it resolves itself
Main won't compile until PR 2 lands; move the callers first instead
The stack is too granular; such migrations must be one combined PR
PR 2 must be approved by a different reviewer than the one for PR 1
explanation: When small changes depend on each other, each one must leave the system working after it is merged; otherwise everyone on main is broken until the next PR lands, possibly for a long time. Reordering the stack (migrate the callers first, delete the old API last) keeps the PRs small and safe, so one huge combined PR is unnecessary.

title: Refactoring code that has no tests
question: You want to restructure a 400-line pricing module that currently has no tests. You plan one PR that both adds characterization tests and restructures the module. What split does Google's guidance suggest?
options: No split; tests and the refactor must always ship together in one change
Refactor first, then add tests later once the new structure is stable
Skip the tests, since a pure refactoring by definition changes no behavior
Land the tests first, then the refactor, so they show behavior is unchanged
explanation: The guidance allows independent test changes to go first, and specifically mentions adding tests for existing untested code before refactoring it, so you can confirm the tested behavior is the same before and after. Pure refactorings still need test coverage, and adding tests after the restructure loses the baseline that would have caught an accidental change.

title: Cache fill in a singleton service
options: Load runs on every request, so the cache never actually takes effect
The key comparison should be case-insensitive to avoid duplicate entries
Concurrent requests write to a non-thread-safe Dictionary and can corrupt it
A singleton cannot keep instance fields, so _rates is reset per request
explanation: A singleton is shared by all concurrent requests, and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> is not safe for concurrent writes: the check-then-act sequence races and simultaneous inserts can corrupt its internal state. Use ConcurrentDictionary (for example GetOrAdd) or proper locking; otherwise the cache does work, and a singleton keeps its fields for the app's lifetime.

title: Swallowing errors in a payment status check
options: Outages look like missing payments, so customers may be charged twice
Catching Exception is slower than catching HttpRequestException alone
Returning null instead of throwing makes the method harder to unit test
The await inside try/catch stops the method from running asynchronously
explanation: Catching every exception and returning a value that callers interpret as a business fact turns timeouts and outages into 'no payment exists', which here leads to duplicate charges. Catch only what you can handle meaningfully and surface failures distinctly; performance and testability are secondary concerns, and await works normally inside try/catch.

title: Per-request data stored in a singleton
question: A PR registers `services.AddSingleton<AuditContext>()` and sets `auditContext.UserId = currentUser.Id` in a middleware; services read it later in the same request to stamp audit rows. Tests pass. What should the reviewer flag?
options: Singletons are created lazily, so the first request will see a null UserId
Middleware cannot resolve singletons; it must take a scoped service instead
Audit rows should be stamped by a database trigger rather than in app code
All requests share one instance, so concurrent users overwrite the id
explanation: A singleton is shared by every request, so storing per-request state in it is a race: under concurrency one request can stamp audit rows with another user's id, which single-user tests never reveal. Per-request data belongs in a scoped service or in HttpContext; middleware can use singletons, and lazy creation is not the issue.

title: Page numbers that skip the first page
question:
The API contract says `page` starts at 1. The PR implements:

query.OrderBy(o => o.Id).Skip(page * size).Take(size)

What will a reviewer reading the contract notice?
options: Take must come before Skip, or EF Core will load the entire table first
Page 1 skips the first `size` rows, so the first page is never returned
OrderBy is unnecessary because Id is already the clustered primary key
Skip and Take are evaluated in memory, after all rows have been fetched
explanation: With 1-based pages the offset must be (page - 1) * size; as written, page 1 already skips one full page, so the first results are unreachable. Checking code against its contract and edge cases is part of reviewing functionality. The operator order is correct, OrderBy is needed for stable paging, and EF Core translates Skip/Take into SQL.

title: Four lines that hide a bigger problem
question: The review tool shows a PR adding four lines to handle a new discount type. Opening the full file, you see they extend a 120-line method that already branches on eight discount types. How should you treat this?
options: Review only the diff; code outside the changed lines is out of scope
Approve, and quietly fix the long method yourself in a follow-up later
Point out the method now needs restructuring, since the PR grows it
Block the PR until the whole discount module is rewritten from scratch
explanation: Google's guidance asks reviewers to look at a change in its broader context: four new lines might look fine alone, but if they grow a method that really needs breaking up, the change adds complexity and the reviewer should say so. Systems usually become complex through many small additions, while demanding a full rewrite is out of proportion.

title: Measuring a timeout with the wall clock
options: Wall-clock time can jump (DST, clock sync); use a monotonic Stopwatch
DateTime.Now has one-second resolution, too coarse for a 30 s budget
Subtracting two DateTime values allocates a heap object per iteration
TimeSpan.FromSeconds runs on each loop and should be a static constant
explanation: DateTime.Now is local wall-clock time, which can jump backwards or forwards on daylight saving transitions or when the system clock is corrected, ending the loop early or running it far too long. Stopwatch (or TimeProvider timestamps) measures elapsed time monotonically. DateTime subtraction yields a struct TimeSpan with no heap allocation, and its resolution is far finer than a second.

title: A test that cannot fail
options: It should use Assert.True with a comparison instead of Assert.Equal
It takes the expected value from the code under test, so bugs pass too
It should mock ShippingFee so the test does not depend on that class
It needs more sample orders, but otherwise it verifies the formula well
explanation: The expected value is computed by the same formula the production code uses, so if the formula is wrong the test still passes: it can never catch the bug it exists for. Reviewers should ask whether tests will actually fail when the code is broken; here that means asserting against independently known values such as hand-calculated fees. Mocking the formula would make the test even more vacuous.

title: An async assertion that always passes
options: ThrowsAsync only works in Theory tests, not in Fact tests
It should catch the exception with try/catch and call Assert.Fail
The returned task is never awaited, so a failure is never observed
ValidationException must be thrown synchronously for this to work
explanation: `Assert.ThrowsAsync` returns a Task; without `await` (inside an `async Task` test) the assertion's outcome is discarded and the test passes even if no exception is thrown. xUnit's analyzer rule xUnit2021 flags exactly this. The fix is to await the assertion in an async test, not a manual try/catch or a Theory.

title: A bug fix with no failing test
question: A PR fixes a crash when an order has zero line items. It changes two lines in `OrderTotals` and touches no tests. What is the most valuable request?
options: Add a test with an empty order that fails before the fix and passes after
Raise the module's coverage target so CI blocks similar changes later on
None; approve it, since a two-line fix is too small to need its own test
Add a code comment describing the crash and the original stack trace
explanation: Google's guidance expects related tests in the same change as the code, and a regression test that reproduces the bug proves the fix works and keeps it fixed. Coverage targets do not guarantee this edge case is exercised, small fixes still need tests, and a comment does not stop the bug from coming back.

title: Raw SQL built with string interpolation
question:
A PR adds a search endpoint with EF Core:

db.Products.FromSqlRaw($"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'")

`term` comes from the query string. What should the reviewer require?
options: Nothing, since EF Core parameterizes every interpolated value automatically
Escape single quotes in term with Replace("'", "''") before building SQL
Wrap the call in a transaction so a malicious query can be rolled back
Use FromSql or LINQ so that term is sent as a real database parameter
explanation: `FromSqlRaw` inserts the interpolated string as-is, so `term` becomes part of the SQL text: a classic SQL injection. `FromSql`/`FromSqlInterpolated`, or plain LINQ such as Contains, send values as DbParameters. Hand-escaping quotes is fragile, and a transaction does not stop data from being read or exfiltrated.

title: Returning exception details to clients
options: Problem details responses must use status 400, not 500, for errors
Stack traces and internals leak to callers; log them server-side
ex.ToString() is slow and should be replaced by ex.Message only
Results.Problem cannot be used inside a global exception handler
explanation: Sending ex.ToString() exposes stack traces, file paths, SQL fragments and library versions to anyone who can trigger an error, which helps attackers map the system. Return a generic problem response (optionally with a correlation id) and log the details on the server. Switching to ex.Message can still leak internals, and 500 is the right status for unexpected errors.

title: Turning off TLS certificate checks
options: Fine for staging only; production traffic is protected by TLS anyway
Acceptable as long as the partner's hostname is pinned in configuration
Move the callback into appsettings so ops can toggle it per environment
It accepts any certificate, enabling interception; fix the trust issue
explanation: Returning true unconditionally disables server certificate validation, so anyone on the network path can present their own certificate and read or alter the traffic; TLS without validation is not protection. Code analysis rule CA5359 flags this pattern. The right fix is the underlying trust problem (missing intermediate, wrong CA, hostname mismatch), not a toggle that can leak into production.

title: Answering 'what does this do?'
question: A reviewer comments on a dense bit-manipulation block: 'I can't tell what this is doing.' What is the best first response from the author?
options: Reply in the review thread with a detailed explanation of the logic
Point the reviewer to the design doc, where the approach is described
Make the code clearer, or add a comment saying why if it can't be
Resolve the thread, since the code is correct and the tests prove it
explanation: If a reviewer cannot understand the code, future readers probably will not either, and an explanation in the review tool helps nobody later. The guidance says to clarify the code itself first and, if it cannot be made clearer, add a code comment explaining why it is there; replying only in the review tool is a last resort.

title: What an 'FYI:' comment means
question: A reviewer writes: 'FYI: the new Span-based parser in .NET could replace this whole helper someday.' How should the author read this label?
options: A blocking request that must be done before the PR can be merged
Something worth knowing for the future, not expected in this PR
A minor polish point that the author technically should still do
A sign the reviewer approves, but only if a follow-up gets filed
explanation: Google's guidance suggests labelling comment severity: 'Nit' is a minor thing you technically should do, 'Optional' or 'Consider' is a suggestion, and 'FYI' means the reviewer does not expect it in this change but it may be interesting for the future. Labels stop authors from treating every comment as mandatory.

title: Disagreeing with a reviewer's request
question: A reviewer asks you to replace an in-memory queue with the company's message broker. You chose the in-memory queue deliberately. Which reply best follows the author guidance?
options: "No, the in-memory queue is fine, and I won't change it in this PR."
"Okay, I'll switch it," although you believe it makes the design worse
"I chose it for latency and ops cost. Is durability your concern?"
"Let's ask the tech lead," before discussing it with the reviewer
explanation: The guidance asks authors to respond collaboratively: explain the trade-offs behind the choice and ask what the reviewer is weighing differently, which usually leads to consensus based on technical facts. A flat refusal is combative, silently complying hides a real disagreement, and escalation comes only after trying to reach consensus.

title: When the author's pushback is right
question: You asked an author to cache a lookup. They reply that the lookup is already served from a process-wide cache one layer down, and link the code. You check and they are right. What should you do?
options: Keep the comment open, since reviewers should not reverse their requests
Ask for the cache anyway as defense in depth, to keep the review consistent
Turn it into a nit so it stays on record without blocking the change
Tell them they are right, drop the request and continue the review
explanation: Google's pushback guidance says to first consider whether the developer is correct, since they are often closer to the code; if their argument makes sense from a code-health perspective, tell them they are right and let the issue drop. Insisting anyway, or leaving it as a lingering nit, wastes effort and erodes trust in the review process.

title: A review thread going in circles
question: An author and a reviewer have exchanged ten comments over three days on whether a module should use events or direct calls, and neither is convinced. What is the recommended next step?
options: Talk on a call, record the outcome on the PR, and escalate if still stuck
Let the PR sit until one side gives up, since forcing it hurts the code
The reviewer approves to unblock things and the author files a ticket
Close the PR and have the author reopen it with a new set of reviewers
explanation: When reaching consensus in comments gets hard, the standard recommends a face-to-face meeting or video call, recording the result as a comment on the change for future readers, and, if that fails, escalating to a broader team discussion, a tech lead, a code maintainer or an engineering manager. It explicitly says not to let a change sit because the two cannot agree.

title: Receiving a harsh review comment
question: A reviewer writes on your PR: 'This is sloppy. Did you even run it?' The underlying issue they point at is real. What does Google's author guidance recommend?
options: Reply in the thread pointing out that the tone is unprofessional
Ignore the comment, since it attacks you personally and not the code
Request a different reviewer and close the thread without replying
Fix the issue; if the tone persists, raise it with them privately
explanation: Authors are advised not to take comments personally: ask what constructive point the reviewer is making, act on that, and never respond in anger in the review tool. If feedback keeps being non-constructive, explain this to the reviewer in person or privately, and escalate to a manager only if that does not work.

title: A CODEOWNERS rule that never applies
question:
A repository's `CODEOWNERS` file contains:

/src/payments/ @org/payments-team
* @org/platform-team

PRs touching `src/payments/` request review only from the platform team. Why?
options: Team handles must be listed before paths in a CODEOWNERS entry
The last matching pattern wins, so * overrides the payments rule
Paths with a leading slash are ignored by GitHub in CODEOWNERS
Code owners are only requested after the pull request leaves draft
explanation: In CODEOWNERS the last matching pattern takes precedence; with the catch-all * placed after the payments rule, every file ends up owned only by the platform team. Put the general rule first and more specific paths after it. A leading slash anchors a pattern to the repository root, and draft status would suppress all owner requests rather than swap teams.

title: Commits pushed after approval
question: On a protected `main`, a PR gets one approval. The author then pushes a commit that adds a new outbound call and merges minutes later without any further review. Which branch protection setting prevents this?
options: Require status checks to pass before merging
Require a linear commit history on the protected branch
Dismiss stale pull request approvals on new commits
Require signed commits on the protected branch
explanation: With 'Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed', GitHub dismisses an approval once the approved diff changes, so the PR needs a fresh approval before merging; 'Require approval of the most recent reviewable push' is a related alternative. Status checks, linear history and signed commits do not ensure a human reviewed the new code.

title: Merge queue stuck waiting for checks
question:
After enabling a merge queue on `main`, PRs enter the queue but never merge; the required `build` check never reports. The workflow has:

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

What is missing?
options: A `merge_group` trigger so the check runs for queued merge groups
A `push` trigger on `main` so the check reruns after each merge
The `pull_request_target` trigger, so the check runs with secrets
A `workflow_dispatch` trigger so maintainers can rerun it by hand
explanation: A merge queue validates temporary branches that combine the latest base branch with the queued PRs, and GitHub Actions only runs required checks for them when the workflow listens to the `merge_group` event; otherwise the required status is never reported and the merge fails. Running on push to main is too late, `pull_request_target` changes the security context, and manual runs do not target the merge group.

title: Reviews dominated by style nits
question: Half of all review comments on a team are about brace placement, import order and spacing, and debates about them delay merges. What is the most effective change?
options: Add a checklist item reminding reviewers to look closely at formatting
Ban style comments entirely and let each author pick their own format
Assign one style reviewer per PR so the others can focus on the logic
Enforce a formatter and linter in CI so humans can focus on design
explanation: Mechanical style rules are best encoded in configuration (for example .editorconfig with dotnet format) and enforced automatically in CI, which keeps formatting consistent and frees reviewers for design, correctness and tests. Checklists and dedicated style reviewers still spend human attention on it, and dropping the standard just moves the inconsistency into the codebase.

title: Analyzer warnings nobody acts on
question: A .NET solution reports CA2100 (SQL injection risk in command text) and CA5359 (disabled certificate validation) warnings, but they get lost among 600 other warnings and keep slipping through review. What is the best automation fix?
options: Set those rules to error in .editorconfig so the build fails on them
Suppress all 600 warnings so that new ones stand out in the output
Add both rule IDs to the PR template so authors check them by hand each time
Run the analyzers weekly and email the full list to the team leads
explanation: Rule severity can be configured per diagnostic in .editorconfig (for example dotnet_diagnostic.CA5359.severity = error), so high-risk findings break the CI build instead of relying on humans to spot them. Blanket suppression hides real issues, and manual checklists or weekly reports keep the problem outside the merge path.

title: Required check pending on docs-only PRs
question: The `tests` workflow is a required status check and is triggered by `pull_request` with `paths: ['src/**']`. A PR that only edits `README.md` shows `tests` as 'Pending' forever and cannot merge. Why?
options: Required checks only run for PRs opened by users with write access
The workflow is skipped by path filtering, so the check never reports
README changes are ignored by Actions unless docs/ is listed as well
The workflow is still queued, waiting for a free GitHub-hosted runner
explanation: When a workflow is skipped by branch or path filtering, the checks associated with it stay 'Pending', and a PR that requires them is blocked from merging. Fixes include not making path-filtered workflows required, or always running the workflow and skipping the expensive steps inside it so it still reports success. It is not a runner capacity or permission issue.
